newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: UK's HMV to put squeeze on Singapore music shops.
newsitem.headline: UK's HMV to put squeeze on Singapore music shops.

text.p: Giant U.K. music retailer HMV's planned entry into Singapore by mid-1997 will put the squeeze on an already highly competitive music retail sector, industry sources said.
"If they adopt a business method similar to what they use in Hong Kong where they slash prices, we would be very frightened," said Peter Quek, owner of DaDa Records in Singapore.
HMV (His Master's Voice) announced last week that it was opening a Singapore $10 million, 25,000-sq-foot store, the largest in the city-state, and was planning more outlets.
"Definitely, some more small shops will go out of business," said Philip Cheah, editor of music magazine BigO.

At stake is the market share of some 300 small- and medium-sized retailers, some of which are already struggling with high costs, a shrinking market and competition from Tower Records, which opened a 12,000-sq-ft music outlet in the heart of Singapore's main shopping district in 1994.
Another music giant, Virgin Records, has changed its mind and will not open in Singapore because it did not see market conditions as favourable, industry sources said.

HMV told a press conference in late October it wanted to be Singapore's number one music retailer. Its offering of 250,000 CDs, more than 200 listening booths and separate rooms for jazz and classicial music are ingredients for stiff competition.
Cheah said the market would see a consolidation among good quality mom-and-pop operations. Observers said small shops that specialise would be the ones to survive.

One retailer said megastores like Tower and HMV would find it hard to compete with the personalised service he gives customers. He said he knew each individual customer's tastes and was able to recommend CDs to them.
Quek said he specialised in music from the 1960s and in collectibles.
Philip Kung, managing director of the HMV Chinese Asia region, told reporters last week that HMV's Singapore business would not all come at the expenses of other retailers.
"We feel there is a market down here. I don't think every dollar of sales will be from someone else. We will be expanding the market as well," said Kung.
"We will not deliberately try to go out and start a price war. We will be very competitive to what is offered in the market place," he said.
He said HMV expected to break even "quite quickly," but did not give a time frame. Tower Records has said it was profitable in its first year of operations here.

According to the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, the Singapore CD market shrank from S$112 million (US$79 million) in 1994 to S$108 million in 1995. For the first six months in 1996, sales were S$55 million.
"It would be interesting to watch if the presence of HMV will increase the music retail market share," said Cheah.
The more optimistic observers said they hoped HMV would improve the quality of the music scene in the city state.
"They will try to have a very comprehensive range of products. It's been sorely lacking in the scene -- that's why the entry of Tower and HMV is good," said Cheah.
Emily Wee, general manager of Tower Records in Singapore, said: "It's good now we will have two big players here to push for better air play on the radio, more exciting acts appearing in town.
"That should help the overall music scene, which has been quite stagnant, getting kind of unexciting, lacklustre of late," she said. "At the end of the day, I don't think they are out to kill us."
